title: Believability of Social Media Posts: A Study of Alleged Forceful Injection of Monkey Pox Virus in School Children
screen_reason: Questionnaire survey of 332 Anambra State (Nigeria) civil servants about the false 11 October 2017 report that Nigerian Army personnel were forcibly injecting schoolchildren with a monkeypox-containing vaccine - a rumour that official reports traced to a single school head's false alarm. The paper reports shares of respondents exposed to the report overall (100%), exposed via social media (85.5%), and by platform (WhatsApp 65.7%, Facebook 16.9%), plus the share who 'alerted others' on first receiving it (49.4%). These are self-reported exposure to, and onward transmission of, a specific piece of misinformation (RECALL). The study's own aim - believability - is out of scope, but the descriptive exposure shares are exactly what the protocol asks us to look for.

estimates.country: Nigeria (Anambra State; civil servants at the State Secretariat, Awka)
estimates.platform: Any channel (social media, colleagues, school authorities, relatives, neighbours)
estimates.date: Not stated; the reported exposure refers to the episode of 11 October 2017; the sampling-frame staff figures are dated 2017; article published 2021
estimates.measure_type: % of surveyed civil servants who reported having been exposed to the false 'Army deadly vaccine / monkeypox injection' report, by any channel
estimates.denominator: 332 civil servants of the Anambra State Secretariat, Awka, who returned the questionnaire (of 341 distributed, 97.4% response)
estimates.definition: Respondent answered Yes to having been exposed to the 11 October 2017 report on the Army 'deadly vaccine' - the authors gloss this as having 'in one way or the other read or heard about the report'
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition. The report is described as a “rumuor” contradicted by official findings: “subsequent official reports showed that the reported deadly vaccine was a mere rumuor which emanated from a school head in Ekwusigo Local Government Area of Anambra State who, on seeing the soldiers who came to the school on a medical outreach, raised the alarm that the soldiers had come to infect the pupils”.
estimates.source_quote: Table 7 Respondents' Exposure to the Army "Deadly Vaccine" Report — Yes 332 (100.0); No 0 (0.0); Total 332 (100.0). "Table 7 shows that all the respondents were exposed to the October 11 2017 report on Army 'deadly vaccine'. Thus, there was 100% exposure to the report, meaning that each of the respondents must have in one way or the other read or heard about the report."
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Falsity of the single target claim is established by the authors from official sources - the 82 Division Nigerian Army's public denial and press reports tracing the rumour to a school head's false alarm. No fact-checker rating, no content coding, no reliability statistic; instrument reliability was checked only by re-administering the questionnaire to 20 pilot respondents after two weeks.
estimates.moderator_quote: The population of the study was civil servants working in the State Secretariat, Awka, from where a sample of 341 was selected. ... Table 2 Sampling Frame ... TOTAL 3,222
estimates.notes: A CEILING value: literally every respondent reported exposure. This is exposure to one locally notorious rumour that shut schools across the state within 48 hours, measured among people who lived through it, so it is not comparable with generic misinformation-exposure items and should not be pooled with them. The item is also a single closed yes/no question asked years after the event, with obvious acquiescence and recall pressure. The other exposure rows below are nested inside this one - do not sum.

estimates.country: Nigeria (Anambra State; civil servants at the State Secretariat, Awka)

estimates.measure_type: % of surveyed civil servants who said their reaction on first getting the false 'deadly vaccine' report was to alert others
estimates.value_raw: 164/332 = 49.4% 'I alerted others' (vs 120 = 36.1% 'I got my wards out of school'; 48 = 14.5% 'I did nothing')
estimates.denominator: 332 civil servants of the Anambra State Secretariat who returned the questionnaire
estimates.definition: Respondent selected 'I alerted others' as their reaction on first receiving the report, i.e. they passed the false report on
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition; the report is treated as a rumour/misinformation refuted by official statements.
estimates.source_quote: Table 18 Respondents' Reaction on First Getting the "Deadly Vaccine" Report — I got my wards out of school 120 (36.1); I alerted others 164 (49.4); I did nothing 48 (14.5); Total 332 (100.0)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: As above; the sharing/alerting behaviour is entirely self-reported and retrospective.
estimates.moderator_quote: most civil servants believed the posts, reacted mainly by bringing their wards back from school and by alerting others of the perceived danger
estimates.notes: Borderline as a SHARING estimate, for two reasons. (1) 'Alerted others' is a reaction category, not a question about resharing a post - it may mean phoning a relative as much as forwarding a message, so this is onward transmission of the false claim rather than platform sharing. (2) The item is single-choice: respondents who took their children out of school could not also be counted as alerting others, so 49.4% is a LOWER bound on how many passed the rumour on. Kept because retrospective self-reported transmission of a specific false claim is exactly recall_subtype=sharing, but it should not be pooled with 'did you share fake news online' items.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted, with reasons. (a) All believability results - 36.7% completely believed the report, 42.8% believed with reservations, 79.5% believed it either way, 91.9% of those who acted did so because they believed it - belief in false claims is out of scope. (b) Table 10 (74.1% said social media was their FIRST source of exposure) - this is about channel ORDER among the already-exposed rather than a distinct exposure prevalence, and it overlaps completely with the 85.5% row; extracting it would triple-count the same event. (c) Tables 14-17 (first non-social-media source; 74.4% of those not initially exposed on social media eventually saw it there; 75.6% for whom social media was the only source) - conditional splits of small subsamples of the same exposure event. (d) Table 12/13 (suspicion of veracity, felt need to confirm) - credibility judgments, not exposure. (e) Social-media access and platform-access shares (93.4% had access; Facebook 83.7%, WhatsApp 78.9%, Instagram 38.6%, Twitter 16.3%, YouTube 34.9%) - media use, not misinformation. (f) 36.1% 'got my wards out of school' - a behavioural response to misinformation, not exposure or sharing. (g) Demographic correlations (Table 21) - associations, not prevalence. DATE UNCERTAINTY: the fieldwork date is nowhere stated; the event is October 2017, the sampling-frame staff numbers are dated 2017 and the article appeared in a Jan-Mar 2021 issue, so 'year' is filled with the publication year as the instructions require, and any temporal analysis should treat this study as referring to an October 2017 event.

rob.design: Cross-sectional questionnaire survey of civil servants in the Anambra State Secretariat, Awka, Nigeria. Population frame 3,222 staff across 13 ministries/departments; proportionate allocation produced a sample of 341; 332 questionnaires recovered (97.4% response, 2.6% loss). Instrument: 21 closed-ended items across demographics, social-media access, exposure, believability and reaction. Validity and reliability assessed only by a 20-person pilot and a two-week test-retest with no statistic reported (no Cronbach's alpha, no kappa). Sample 50.9% male, 60.8% first degree/HND. Analysis is descriptive frequencies plus zero-order correlations. Fieldwork date not reported; exposure is retrospective self-report about a single October 2017 event, so recall and social-desirability bias are unquantified. The 100% exposure figure indicates a ceiling/acquiescence problem.
